images.prompt: Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama. A graphite clipboard, about the size of a paperback, lies squarely on a pale neutral tabletop. Its clip holds a form set: a crisp ivory top sheet with blank ruled fields, then two thinner, slightly translucent copy sheets below it, separated by whisper-thin graphite carbon leaves whose edges peek out in a neat stepped fringe. An acid-lime perforation strip runs across the top of the set, where the copies are meant to tear apart. To the left, a graphite pen rests on a small stand; to the right, three shallow graphite trays wait, one for each copy. Fine fibres lift along the perforation, and faint grey smudges mark the carbon edges. Everything is square and aligned. Wide 16:9 landscape frame. The hero object sits slightly left of centre on the lower third, with the related objects extending to the right so the workflow reads left to right. Clean, generous negative space above. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: one large soft key light from the upper left at about 45 degrees, like diffused north-window daylight, with a gentle white bounce fill from the right; soft grounded contact shadows fall to the lower right. Camera: 100mm macro lens at f/4, eye level with the tabletop, three-quarter view. The hero object is tack sharp and the background melts into smooth, creamy blur on a seamless pale neutral sweep. Mood: calm, precise, orderly and quietly premium, like high-end editorial product photography. Strictly no people, figures, faces, hands or silhouettes. No readable text, letters, numbers, clock digits, logos, signage or user-interface graphics anywhere. No holograms, floating screens, robots with faces, dense cable tangles, carnival or circus elements, cartoon or plastic CGI look, oversaturated colour, lens flare or heavy vignette.

Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama, captured mid-disaster. The same clipboard is now the base of a towering stack. Every form has spawned three more: sheets peel off in threes and pile upward, the stack leaning back over the clipboard far above the pen stand. The three trays are buried and overflowing, and loose carbon leaves have slipped out and fluttered down, leaving smudged grey streaks across the tabletop. Near the top, sheets are frozen mid-air, lifting and splitting apart in fans of three. The acid-lime perforation strip on the original set is still intact at the very bottom, pressed flat under the load and never torn. The clip has bent open under the weight, and the pen has been knocked from its stand and rolls toward the edge. Wide 16:9 landscape frame, same layout and angle as the calm version of this scene. The hero object stays slightly left of centre, and the spread of the disaster runs to the right and toward the camera so its path can be traced back to the source. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: the same soft upper-left key and right-side bounce fill as a calm studio setup, unchanged, so the disorder reads as physical and real rather than theatrical. Airborne paper, grains and fragments catch the key light with crisp edge highlights. Camera: 85mm lens at f/5.6, same three-quarter tabletop angle, fast shutter freezing everything mid-air. Focus sits where the chain reaction started, and the spread softens into the depth of field. Mood: absurd but plausible, an orderly system that got out of hand, still clean and editorial. Photorealistic photograph of a vast handcrafted miniature landscape diorama. A grey-ivory tableland of compacted forms stretches to a hazy horizon, eroded into flat-topped mesas whose cliff walls show thousands of thin layered sheets, darker bands marking the pressed carbon leaves between them. At the foot of the nearest mesa lies the old clipboard, now as large as a hangar door, its clip bent upward like a broken arch. The three trays sit half buried as sunken courtyards. Loose sheets lift off the mesa tops, frozen in the wind. In the foreground, a slim graphite binding rig on four long legs has drawn one single form set out of the cliff wall and clamps it inside a small graphite binder with an acid-lime spine, setting it on a clean plinth. Dust lines each ledge. Wide 16:9 panoramic frame. The main ruin anchors the left or centre foreground, terrain rolls back to a distant horizon on the upper third, and the lime recovery rig sits in the right midground. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents.
